content: Ranitidine is a medication classified as a histamine H2-receptor antagonist, which works by reducing the production of stomach acid. It is widely used in the management of conditions such as peptic ulcer disease (PUD) and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). The drug is available over the counter under brand names like Zinetac and Zantac, marketed by GlaxoSmithKline and other pharmaceutical companies under various trade names. In terms of clinical availability, certain formulations of ranitidine can be purchased without a prescription in many countries. In the United States, over-the-counter options include 75 mg and 150 mg tablets. In Australia, 150 mg tablets are sold in packs of 7 or 14 doses in supermarkets, while small packs of 150 mg and 300 mg tablets are classified as Schedule 2 Pharmacy Medicines, meaning they are available without a prescription but must be sold in pharmacies. Larger doses or pack sizes still require a prescription. Outside the United States, ranitidine is sometimes combined with bismuth as a citrate salt (ranitidine bismuth citrate, marketed as Tritec) to treat infections caused by Helicobacter pylori. This combination is typically administered alongside clarithromycin, an antibiotic, to enhance the eradication of the bacteria. Ranitidine was developed by Glaxo, now known as GlaxoSmithKline, as part of an effort to improve upon the first histamine H2-receptor antagonist, cimetidine, which was created by Smith, Kline & French (also now part of GlaxoSmithKline). The development of ranitidine involved a rational drug-design process that utilized an advanced understanding of the histamine H2-receptor and quantitative structure-activity relationships (QSAR). Glaxo modified the chemical structure of cimetidine by replacing its imidazole ring with a furan ring containing a nitrogen-based substituent. This structural change resulted in ranitidine, which demonstrated several advantages over cimetidine, including a significantly improved tolerability profile (fewer adverse drug reactions), a longer duration of action, and a potency that was ten times greater than that of cimetidine. Additionally, ranitidine exhibited a reduced affinity for the cytochrome P450 enzyme system, with only 10% of the interaction seen with cimetidine. This reduced interaction with P450 enzymes led to fewer drug-drug interactions and side effects. However, other H2-receptor antagonists, such as famotidine and nizatidine, have no significant interactions with the P450 system at all. Ranitidine was first introduced to the market in 1981 and quickly became the world’s best-selling prescription drug by 1988. Despite its initial success, ranitidine has largely been replaced by proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), such as omeprazole, which are more effective in reducing stomach acid production. Omeprazole, in particular, went on to become one of the best-selling drugs globally for many years.
